title: Measurements: singular substance
summary: Use a singular partitive substance after a container or measurement word.
objectives: Use a singular partitive substance after a container or measurement word.

sections.title: Meaning and pattern
paragraphs: Use a singular partitive substance after a container or measurement word.
The measurement word supplies the unit. The following noun names the contents. A precise measure does not remove the partitive from that contents noun.
The measurement itself is provided in its basic form. Changing the measurement into another case is outside this lesson.
keyPoints: The substance following this measure uses singular partitive. The measure names the amount; the next noun names what is measured.

steps: The substance following this measure uses singular partitive. The measure names the amount; the next noun names what is measured.
Litra means “litre” and works as the quantity word. litra is used in its displayed form here; no additional ending is needed.
maitoa means “milk” and works as the singular partitive noun naming counted items or a measured amount. Keep maito and add -a: maito + a = maitoa.
The substance following this measure uses singular partitive. The measure names the amount; the next noun names what is measured.
Kuppi means “cup” and works as the noun in its dictionary form naming the unit of measurement. kuppi is the dictionary form, with no case ending added.
kahvia means “coffee” and works as the singular partitive noun naming counted items or a measured amount. This i-word keeps i: kahvi + a = kahvia. The back vowel a determines the ending.
The substance following this measure uses singular partitive. The measure names the amount; the next noun names what is measured.
Lasi means “glass” and works as the quantity word. lasi is used in its displayed form here; no additional ending is needed.
mehua means “juice” and works as the singular partitive noun naming counted items or a measured amount. Keep mehu and add -a: mehu + a = mehua.
The substance following this measure uses singular partitive. The measure names the amount; the next noun names what is measured.
Kilo means “kilogram” and works as the quantity word. kilo is used in its displayed form here; no additional ending is needed.
juustoa means “cheese” and works as the singular partitive noun naming counted items or a measured amount. Keep juusto and add -a: juusto + a = juustoa.

commonMistakes: An exact litre still uses a partitive contents noun.
Keep the measurement word and its contents separate.
